verdict.reasoning: Patient reports waking up with a “really horrible pain on the left side of my head” that “woke me up quite early this morning… probably around 5:30ish,” confirming sudden onset, left‑sided, and that it woke him from sleep. Severity as ‘really horrible’ supports describing it as severe.

Transcript confirms the headache is still present and worse on initially lying down (“it kind of feels a little bit sore at first and it takes me a while to get comfortable”), but it does not explicitly state that the headache has been constant or specifically ‘worse on waking’ compared to later in the morning.
Patient states being “a little bit sensitive” to bright lights, which “makes my eyes a little bit sore, but nothing that I can't really handle,” consistent with mild photophobia.
Patient reports “when I first got up this morning my head felt a bit dizzy, but that's kind of… seems to be fine,” indicating transient, minimal early dizziness associated with the headache onset.

Doctor asks, “are you feeling nauseous at all?” and patient answers, “Not really… my head felt a bit dizzy… but… seems to be fine,” with no mention of vomiting; absence of nausea/vomiting is consistent with the fact.
Doctor asks, “do you have any fever?” and patient replies, “No,” directly supporting no fever with the headache.
Doctor asks, “Do you have any neck stiffness at all?” and patient replies, “No,” supporting absence of neck stiffness.

Patient says that when lying down “it kind of feels a little bit sore at first… at the beginning it does, but then again, that just kind of soothes a little bit,” and agrees it is ultimately better when lying down, indicating improvement after settling supine.
Patient reports having “taken some paracetamol” and when asked if it helped says, “Not really, no,” showing paracetamol has been ineffective.

Patient notes a “bit of a history with headaches but nothing as severe as this,” previously “a bit of a cluster at the front of my head,” whereas this time it is “more prominent on the left side, which I've never really had,” supporting that prior headaches were frontal and milder, not similar unilateral headaches.

Patient describes work as “kind of a bit stressful… lot of kind of a backlog of work… doing a lot of late nights,” and when asked duration says, “Probably about a couple of months now,” supporting increased work stress for ~2 months with late nights.
Patient says, “I had, like, anxiety for about two years now and I've been on Sertraline for a while,” consistent with a history of generalized anxiety disorder.
Doctor asks, “Are you taking sertraline at the moment?” and patient replies, “Yes,” confirming current sertraline use.
Patient reports taking “some paracetamol” for this headache and “No, that's it. Just paracetamol,” indicating paracetamol use as needed.
When asked about allergies, patient says, “Not that I'm aware of, no,” supporting no known drug allergies.
Patient states, “My mum's had a history of anxiety as well,” confirming maternal anxiety.
Doctor asks if anyone in the family has migraines and patient answers, “No, they haven't,” supporting no reported family history of migraine.
When asked about living situation, patient says, “I live with my partner,” confirming this.
Doctor asks, “Are you a smoker?” and patient replies, “No,” confirming non‑smoker status.
In response to exercise, patient states, “normally I try to go running at least three times a week,” supporting running ~3 times per week.
When asked about pets, patient answers, “I have a cat,” confirming a cat at home.
Patient describes work as “kind of a bit stressful… got a lot going on… backlog of work… doing a lot of late nights,” which supports that the job has a high workload.

Doctor states it “might be one of two things… tension headache… The other possibility is migraine as well,” and explicitly checks for fever and neck stiffness (both denied) and mentions following danger signs sheet; this supports assessment of acute unilateral headache with possible migraine vs tension-type and no red-flag features reported.

Doctor links tension headache to “you've been under some pressure and you have a history of anxiety,” and patient reports only situational work anxiety (“don't feel massively anxious”), indicating stress/anxiety are contributory while overall anxiety is reasonably stable on sertraline.

Doctor says, “the things that we start off first line if someone had migraine would be to start ibuprofen. And the doses of ibuprofen can be a bit more than the normal dosage… You can keep on taking paracetamol as well if you like, but the ibuprofen is actually more effective,” matching high-dose ibuprofen per guideline and possibly continuing paracetamol.
Doctor advises “ensure that you're having a minimum of 7, 8 hours sleep at night, every night… A minimum of 1.5 to 2 liters of water or fluids a day,” which matches the stated recommendation.

Doctor says, “I'll also leave a link to some of the danger signs and symptoms of headaches in the notes… what kind of things should trigger you contacting another doctor,” and earlier advises a “low threshold for ringing us back,” aligning with written red‑flag advice and low threshold to re‑present.

Doctor says, “If we're finding that things are not getting better, we might need to arrange some blood tests or look at other possibilities,” but does not explicitly mention imaging. Follow-up is planned, but imaging is not stated.

Doctor suggests, “maybe consider taking some time off work… maybe having a week off if you self certify that might help with things,” which matches a one‑week self‑certified sick leave to reduce workload stress.
Doctor says, “there's counseling service in your area that I can give you the link for you to self refer,” confirming signposting to a self‑referral counseling service.

Doctor mentions providing a link to “danger signs and symptoms of headaches” but does not enumerate specific items such as “severe worsening, neurological deficits, persistent vomiting, and visual changes,” so these specific examples are not in the transcript.
Doctor states, “we'll have a follow up in a week's time… we'll touch base in a week's time with me, myself, or one of the other doctors,” implying a planned tele-consult follow-up in one week.
